contentBlocks.text: Last year you added small groups together by counting everything from the start. This year we'll learn a faster way: counting on. It's a strategy real mathematicians use every day!

To count on, start with the bigger number and count up by the smaller one. For 8 + 3: start at 8, then count up three more: 9, 10, 11. So 8 + 3 = 11! This is much faster than counting all 11 objects from scratch. Try it with 12 + 4: start at 12, count up four: 13, 14, 15, 16. So 12 + 4 = 16.
Counting on is a strategy you'll use constantly in math. Practice starting with the bigger number every time — it saves you counting steps!

objectives: Add two numbers within 20 using the counting-on strategy
Recognize that starting from the larger number is more efficient than counting both groups from the start
materialsNeeded: Optional: a number line or number chart 1-20 for visual support
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review how addition worked last year (counting a whole combined group).
2. Introduce counting on: start at the bigger number, count up by the smaller one.
3. Model 8 + 3 together, counting on fingers or a number line: 9, 10, 11.
4. Try 2-3 more examples together, always identifying the bigger number first.
5. Move to the worksheet: solve each problem using counting on.
6. Close by asking the child to explain the counting-on strategy in their own words.
differentiationTips: Struggling: use a physical number line and have the child hop forward the smaller number of times
Ready for more: try counting-on problems where the numbers are close together (like 9+8) to build fluency with larger jumps
For a child who already knows some addition facts by memory, ask them to double-check their memorized answer using counting on
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Counting on is a core Grade 1 addition strategy (matching the Common Core 1.OA.5 fluency-building progression) that builds toward memorized addition facts and prepares students for subtraction-as-counting-back later this week.

generationData.instructions: Use counting on (start at the bigger number, then count up) to solve each problem.
